title: Bowls that only curve up
objectives: Test a matrix for positive definiteness in several ways.
Tell a bowl from a trough and a saddle by the signs of the eigenvalues.

screens.title: A number from a matrix
screens.prose: For $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{x} = (x, y)$, multiply out $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = 2x^2 + 2xy + 2y^2$. The rings are where it equals 1 and 4. Drag P and read its value in the caption.
screens.question: What is $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ at $\mathbf{x} = (1, -1)$?

hints.text: Drag P to $(1, -1)$, or put $x = 1$, $y = -1$ into the formula.
The cross term $2xy$ is negative here.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $x = 1$ and $y = -1$ into $2x^2 + 2xy + 2y^2$.

byKey.plus: You used $(1, 1)$, where the cross term adds. At $(1, -1)$ it subtracts.
byKey.no-cross: You dropped the cross term $2xy$. Both off-diagonal 1s contribute to it.
byKey.half-cross: You counted the off-diagonal entry once. It appears twice in $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$, giving $2xy$.

explain.text: At $(1, -1)$ the cross term $-2$ cancels one square, leaving 2. Each off-diagonal entry adds $xy$, so the two give $2xy$. P sits on the ring where the value is 2, between the two drawn rings.

screens.title: Slide the corner entries
screens.prose: Now $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}2&b\\b&2\end{pmatrix}$, so $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = 2x^2 + 2bxy + 2y^2$. Blue rings are where it equals 1 and 4. Amber curves are where it equals $-1$ and $-4$. Slide $b$.

derive.caption: $b$ = {{b}}: the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A}$ are {{2 + b}} and {{2 - b}}

screens.question: For which $b$ are the blue curves closed rings round the origin?

options.why: You tried only positive $b$. At $b = -1$ the rings close too, and at $b = 2.5$ they open.
You included the ends. At $b = 2$ the rings open into parallel lines: a trough.
Slide past 2. The amber curves appear: the value goes negative, so the bowl is gone.

hints.text: Watch the caption as the rings open. Which eigenvalue reaches 0?

feedback.correct: Both eigenvalues $2 \pm b$ are positive exactly when $-2 < b < 2$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide $b$ to 2 and to $-2$, and watch the rings.

explain.text: Inside $-2 < b < 2$ both eigenvalues are positive and the rings close: a bowl. At $b = \pm 2$ one eigenvalue is 0 and the rings become parallel lines: a trough. Beyond that one eigenvalue is negative, and the bowl becomes a saddle.

screens.title: The lowest point on the circle
screens.prose: When $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} > 0$ for every $\mathbf{x} \neq \mathbf{0}$, $\mathbf{A}$ is **positive definite**: its graph is a bowl. How steep is the bowl's shallowest side? Take $b = 1.5$. P rides the unit circle.
screens.question: What is the smallest value of $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ on the unit circle?

widget.label: Smallest value on the unit circle

hints.text: Drag P all the way round and watch the caption.
The value is lowest on the diagonal through $(1, -1)$.

feedback.correct: 0.5, at $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1, -1)$, the eigenvector of the smaller eigenvalue.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag P round the whole circle and take the lowest reading.

byKey.largest: That is the largest value, at $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1, 1)$. Keep going round to the other diagonal.
byKey.start: That is the value where P started, at $(1, 0)$. Drag it round the circle.
byKey.zero: Zero happens only at the origin, which is off the circle. On the circle the bowl is at least 0.5 high.

explain.text: The lowest reading, 0.5, came at the unit eigenvector $\mathbf{q}_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1, -1)$. There $\mathbf{q}_2^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{q}_2 = \lambda_2\,\mathbf{q}_2^T\mathbf{q}_2 = 0.5$. So the bowl's flattest direction is the eigenvector of the smallest eigenvalue.

screens.title: A test by elimination
screens.prose: Eigenvalues are slow to find for big matrices. Elimination is quicker. For a symmetric matrix, the pivots are positive exactly when the eigenvalues are. Eliminate $\mathbf{A}$ from the first screen.
screens.question: What is the second pivot?

hints.text: Subtract $\tfrac{1}{2}$ of row 1 from row 2.
Row 2 is $(1, 2)$ and half of row 1 is $(1, \tfrac{1}{2})$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract half of row 1 from row 2, then read the new diagonal entry.

byKey.full-row: You subtracted all of row 1. The multiplier is $\tfrac{1}{2}$, so only half of the 1 comes off.
byKey.eigen: That is the larger eigenvalue. Pivots and eigenvalues differ, but they agree in sign.
byKey.added: You added half of row 1. Elimination subtracts it, to clear the entry below the pivot.

explain.text: Pivots 2 and 1.5 are both positive, as the eigenvalues 3 and 1 are. Their product, 3, is $\det\mathbf{A}$, and so is $3 \times 1$. For $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{pmatrix}$, the second pivot is $c - b^2/a$.

screens.title: Corner determinants
screens.prose: The pivots can be read from determinants. Take the top-left $1 \times 1$, $2 \times 2$ and $3 \times 3$ corners of $\mathbf{K}$, the **leading** submatrices. All their determinants are positive exactly when $\mathbf{K}$ is positive definite.
screens.question: Fill in the three leading determinants.

hints.text: The $2 \times 2$ corner is $\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$.
Expand the $3 \times 3$ along the first row; the 0 kills one term.

feedback.correct: 2, 3 and 4: all positive, so $\mathbf{K}$ is positive definite.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute each corner's determinant in turn.

byKey.r1c1: Your $2 \times 2$ is off: $2 \times 2 - (-1)(-1) = 3$. The two $-1$s multiply to $+1$.
byKey.r0c1: The $1 \times 1$ corner is just the entry 2.

explain.text: The determinants are 2, 3 and 4. Each pivot is a ratio of them: $2$, $\tfrac{3}{2}$ and $\tfrac{4}{3}$. All positive, so $\mathbf{K}$ is positive definite: its eigenvalues are $2 - \sqrt{2}$, 2 and $2 + \sqrt{2}$.

screens.title: A matrix times its transpose
screens.prose: A last test builds the bowl directly. If $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{R}^T\mathbf{R}$, then $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = (\mathbf{R}\mathbf{x})^T(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{x}) = |\mathbf{R}\mathbf{x}|^2 \ge 0$. Here $\mathbf{R}$ is $3 \times 2$.
screens.question: Fill in $\mathbf{R}^T\mathbf{R}$.

hints.text: Entry $(i, j)$ is column $i$ of $\mathbf{R}$ dotted with column $j$.
The columns of $\mathbf{R}$ are $(1, 1, 0)$ and $(0, 1, 1)$.

feedback.correct: $\mathbf{R}^T\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{A}$, the matrix from the first screen.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Dot the columns of $\mathbf{R}$ with each other.

byKey.r0c1: Your top-left entry is off: column 1 dotted with itself is $1 + 1 + 0 = 2$.
byKey.r1c2: Your bottom-right entry is off: column 2 dotted with itself is $0 + 1 + 1 = 2$.
byKey.r0c2: Your off-diagonal entry is off: the columns share only the middle 1, so the dot product is 1.
byKey.r1c1: Your off-diagonal entry is off: the columns share only the middle 1, so the dot product is 1.

explain.text: $\mathbf{R}^T\mathbf{R}$ is $\mathbf{A}$ again. At $\mathbf{x} = (1, -1)$, $\mathbf{R}\mathbf{x} = (1, 0, -1)$ and $|\mathbf{R}\mathbf{x}|^2 = 2$, as on the first screen. $\mathbf{R}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ only for $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$, because the columns are independent.

screens.title: Positive entries
screens.prose: Every entry of $\mathbf{T} = \begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$ is positive. Its form is $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{T}\mathbf{x} = x^2 + 4xy + y^2$. Drag P to test it.
screens.question: Is $\mathbf{T}$ positive definite?

options.why: You read positive entries as a positive matrix. The test is about $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{T}\mathbf{x}$: try P at $(1, -1)$.

options.text: Yes: both diagonal entries are positive
options.why: You checked only the axes, where the value is $x^2$ or $y^2$. Off the axes the $4xy$ term can win.
You used $2xy$, counting the off-diagonal 2 once. It counts twice: $4xy = -4$, so the value is $1 - 4 + 1 = -2$.

hints.text: Positive definite needs a positive value at every $\mathbf{x} \neq \mathbf{0}$. Look for one that fails.
Make $xy$ negative: try P at $(1, -1)$.

feedback.correct: $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{T}\mathbf{x} = -2$ at $(1, -1)$, so $\mathbf{T}$ is not positive definite.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag P to $(1, -1)$ and read the value.

byKey.entries: You read positive entries as a positive definite matrix. At $(1, -1)$ the value is $1 - 4 + 1 = -2$. The eigenvalues are 3 and $-1$.

explain.text: At $(1, -1)$ the cross term $-4$ beats the squares: $1 - 4 + 1 = -2$. The eigenvalues are 3 and $-1$, and the second pivot is $1 - 4 = -3$. The contours are a saddle, not a bowl.

screens.title: Five ways to say bowl
screens.prose:
For a symmetric $\mathbf{A}$, each test implies the others:
- $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} > 0$ for every $\mathbf{x} \neq \mathbf{0}$
- every eigenvalue is positive
- every pivot is positive
- every leading determinant is positive
- $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{R}^T\mathbf{R}$ with independent columns

With $\ge 0$ for $> 0$, $\mathbf{A}$ is **positive semidefinite**: a trough is allowed.
screens.question: Is $\begin{pmatrix}3&5\\5&9\end{pmatrix}$ positive definite?

options.text: Yes: the leading determinants are 3 and 2
No: the off-diagonal 5 is bigger than the diagonal 3
options.why: You compared one corner with one diagonal entry. The test is $3 \times 9 - 5^2 = 2 > 0$.

options.text: No: the determinant is $27 - 10 = 17$, too far from 0
options.why: You subtracted $2 \times 5$, not $5^2$. And any positive determinant passes, with $3 > 0$.
You reached for eigenvalues. Any one test settles it, and determinants are quickest here.

hints.text: Use the leading determinants: the top-left entry, then the whole determinant.

explain.text: Both leading determinants, 3 and 2, are positive, so it is a bowl. The bowl is narrow: the eigenvalues are about 11.83 and 0.17. A positive determinant alone would not do: it also fits two negative eigenvalues.

screens.title: Why the eigenvalue test works
screens.prose: Take a symmetric $2 \times 2$ $\mathbf{A}$ with orthonormal eigenvectors $\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2$ and eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \lambda_2$. We rewrite $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ in the eigenvector basis.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $\mathbf{x} = c_1\mathbf{q}_1 + c_2\mathbf{q}_2$, since $\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2$ are a basis
$\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = c_1\lambda_1\mathbf{q}_1 + c_2\lambda_2\mathbf{q}_2$, since each $\mathbf{q}_i$ is an eigenvector
This is $> 0$ for every $\mathbf{x} \neq \mathbf{0}$ exactly when $\lambda_1 > 0$ and $\lambda_2 > 0$

hints.text: Express $\mathbf{x}$ first, then apply $\mathbf{A}$.
The cross terms vanish because the eigenvectors are perpendicular.
Basis, apply $\mathbf{A}$, dot, simplify, read the sign.

feedback.correct: In the eigenvector basis the form is a weighted sum of squares.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $\mathbf{x}$ in the eigenvector basis before applying $\mathbf{A}$.

byKey.ortho: The simplification needs the dot product written out first. Put the dotting line before it.
byKey.apply: You applied $\mathbf{A}$ before $\mathbf{x}$ was written in the eigenvector basis. Start with the basis.

explain.text: The perpendicular eigenvectors killed the cross terms, leaving $\lambda_1c_1^2 + \lambda_2c_2^2$. Taking $c_2 = 0$ shows $\lambda_1 > 0$ is needed, and likewise $\lambda_2$. With $\lambda_2 = 0$ the form is 0 along $\mathbf{q}_2$: semidefinite, a trough.

screens.title: A hedge with a flat bottom
screens.prose: You hedge a position with $h_1$ and $h_2$ units of two index futures. The leftover variance is a quadratic in $\mathbf{h}$ whose Hessian is $2\mathbf{S}$. Here $\mathbf{S}$ is the futures' covariance matrix, in $\%^2$.
screens.question: Is there exactly one best hedge?

options.text: No: $\det\mathbf{S} = 0$, so the bowl has a flat direction
Yes: every entry of $\mathbf{S}$ is positive
options.why: You read positive entries as a bowl again. Check the determinant: $36 - 36 = 0$.

options.text: Yes: both variances, 4 and 9, are positive
options.why: You checked the diagonal only. The second leading determinant, $4 \times 9 - 6^2$, is 0.

options.text: No: the variance has a saddle, so no minimum
options.why: You took $\det = 0$ as negative. The eigenvalues are 13 and 0: a trough, not a saddle.

hints.text: Run the leading determinant test on $\mathbf{S}$.
$4 > 0$, but what is $4 \times 9 - 6^2$?
$\det\mathbf{S} = 0$, so $\mathbf{S}$ is only semidefinite: one eigenvalue is 0.

feedback.correct: $\det\mathbf{S} = 0$: semidefinite, so the best hedges form a line.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test whether $\mathbf{S}$ is positive definite or only semidefinite.

explain.text: $\mathbf{S}(3, -2) = (0, 0)$: long 3 of the first future and short 2 of the second has zero variance. The second future moves 1.5 times the first, so they are redundant. Adding $(3, -2)$ to any best hedge gives another best hedge.

ideas: $\mathbf{A}$ is positive definite when $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} > 0$ for every $\mathbf{x} \neq \mathbf{0}$: its graph is a bowl.
For symmetric $\mathbf{A}$ the tests agree: positive eigenvalues, positive pivots, positive leading determinants, or $\mathbf{R}^T\mathbf{R}$ with independent columns.
Semidefinite allows 0: a trough with a flat direction, where some $\mathbf{x} \neq \mathbf{0}$ gives $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = 0$.

formula.name: The form in the eigenvector basis
formula.note: Here $\mathbf{x} = c_1\mathbf{q}_1 + c_2\mathbf{q}_2$. Every $\lambda_i > 0$ gives a bowl.

summary.trap: Positive entries do not make a bowl: $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues 3 and $-1$, and $(1, -1)$ gives $-2$.

quiz.prose: A diagonal matrix has its eigenvalues on the diagonal.
quiz.question: Which diagonal matrix is positive definite?

options.why: You may have counted two positives out of three. The $-1$ makes $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = -1$ at $(0, 1, 0)$.
You treated 0 as positive. At $(0, 1, 0)$ the value is 0: semidefinite only.
You may have looked at sizes, not signs. The $-0.5$ gives a negative value at $(0, 1, 0)$.

feedback.correct: 3, 0.01 and 2 are all positive, small or not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A diagonal matrix is positive definite exactly when every diagonal entry is positive.

explain.text: For a diagonal matrix, $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{D}\mathbf{x} = d_1x_1^2 + d_2x_2^2 + d_3x_3^2$. This is positive for every $\mathbf{x} \neq \mathbf{0}$ exactly when every $d_i > 0$. A tiny 0.01 still counts.

quiz.question: What is the smallest whole number $a$ that makes $\mathbf{A}$ positive definite?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the determinant: $2a - 3^2 > 0$.

byKey.corner: At $a = 4$ the determinant is $8 - 9 = -1$. Bigger than the off-diagonal 3 is not enough.

explain.text: The leading determinants are $a$ and $2a - 9$. Both are positive when $a > 4.5$. The smallest whole number is 5, giving determinant 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract $\tfrac{2}{4}$ of row 1 from row 2.

byKey.full: You subtracted all of row 1: $3 - 2 = 1$. The multiplier is $\tfrac{2}{4} = \tfrac{1}{2}$, so subtract half of it.
byKey.det: 8 is $\det\mathbf{A}$, the product of the pivots 4 and 2. The second pivot alone is $8/4 = 2$.

explain.text: The multiplier is $\tfrac{2}{4} = \tfrac{1}{2}$. Row 2 becomes $(2, 3) - \tfrac{1}{2}(4, 2) = (0, 2)$. Pivots 4 and 2 multiply to $\det\mathbf{A} = 8$.

quiz.prose: $\mathbf{R} = \begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$ has a second column twice its first. Let $\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{R}^T\mathbf{R}$.
quiz.question: Which is true of $\mathbf{M}$?

options.text: Positive definite: it has the form $\mathbf{R}^T\mathbf{R}$
options.why: You forgot the condition on the columns. $\mathbf{R}(2, -1) = \mathbf{0}$, so $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x} = 0$ there.

options.text: Neither: some $\mathbf{x}$ gives a negative value
options.why: You may have seen the zero determinant as a sign change. $|\mathbf{R}\mathbf{x}|^2$ is never negative.
You confused one zero direction with every direction. $\mathbf{M} = \begin{pmatrix}5&10\\10&20\end{pmatrix}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for an $\mathbf{x} \neq \mathbf{0}$ with $\mathbf{R}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x} = |\mathbf{R}\mathbf{x}|^2 \ge 0$ always. But $\mathbf{R}(2, -1) = (0, 0)$, so the value is 0 there. $\mathbf{M}$ is semidefinite, with eigenvalues 25 and 0.
